body:
Why a hazard does not always become a disaster

Earthquakes, floods, cyclones, droughts and industrial accidents can threaten human life and property. However, the occurrence of a dangerous natural or human-induced event does not necessarily mean that a disaster has occurred. The consequences depend on what lies in the affected area, how susceptible it is to damage and how effectively people can cope.

A hazard is a process, phenomenon or human activity that has the potential to cause loss of life, injury, damage to property, social or economic disruption, or environmental degradation.

A strong earthquake beneath an uninhabited area is a hazardous event. The same earthquake affecting a densely populated settlement with unsafe buildings may produce a major disaster. The earthquake is the hazard; the disruption and losses arise from its interaction with people, assets and their circumstances.

Under section 2(d) of India's Disaster Management Act, 2005, a disaster involves a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence arising from natural or human-made causes, accident or negligence, producing serious losses or damage of a nature or magnitude beyond the coping capacity of the affected community. The 2025 amendment clarifies that law-and-order-related situations are excluded from the expression human-made causes for this definition.

Basic classification of hazards

  • Geological or geophysical hazards: earthquakes and certain landslides.
  • Hydrometeorological hazards: cyclones, floods, droughts, heatwaves and storm surges.
  • Biological hazards: disease-causing organisms and related biological threats.
  • Technological or industrial hazards: toxic gas releases, factory explosions, chemical spills and infrastructure failures.

Some hazards involve more than one category or have both natural and human influences. For example, heavy rainfall may initiate flooding, while blocked drainage and unplanned construction can increase its consequences.

The 4 essential components of disaster risk

Disaster risk means the potential losses and disruption that may occur over a specified period. It concerns possible future harm, not only damage that has already happened. The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 expressly defines disaster risk as a function of hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity.

ComponentMeaningCoastal cyclone example
HazardPotentially damaging process or eventStrong winds and storm surge
ExposurePeople or assets located where the hazard can occurHouses, roads and fishing boats near the coast
VulnerabilityConditions that increase susceptibility to harmWeak roofs, limited savings or difficulty evacuating
CapacityStrengths, skills, institutions and resources available to manage riskWarnings, trained volunteers, safe shelters and transport

Exposure and vulnerability are not the same

A house on a floodplain is exposed because of its location. Its susceptibility to damage depends on its vulnerability, which may be influenced by building condition, access to safe water and the ability of its occupants to leave before flooding.

Two households may face the same floodwater but experience different consequences. A household that receives timely warnings, has a safe evacuation route and can reach a shelter may suffer less harm. The location determines exposure; the circumstances of the household influence vulnerability and capacity.

Vulnerability can be physical, social, economic or environmental. Poverty, inaccessible warning messages, poor health, limited mobility and damaged ecosystems may increase risk in particular circumstances. Vulnerability is therefore not simply another word for exposure or for the hazard's strength.

How the components interact

Higher hazard severity, greater exposure and greater vulnerability generally increase disaster risk. Effective capacity can reduce the likely consequences. This relationship is conceptual: it is not a universal numerical formula in which every factor can always be multiplied or divided using the same units.

A hazard's physical intensity does not, by itself, determine whether an event becomes a disaster. Exposure, vulnerability and coping capacity also matter.

Prelims focus

  • Hazard: potential source of harm.
  • Exposure: people and assets in hazard-prone locations.
  • Vulnerability: conditions increasing susceptibility to harm.
  • Capacity: available strengths and resources for managing risk.
  • The Disaster Management Act, 2005 defines disaster with reference to the affected community's coping capacity.
  • Trap: A hazardous event is not automatically a disaster.

[Sources: Disaster Management Act, 2005, section 2(d) and 2(e); Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, section 2, amendments to the definitions of disaster, disaster risk, hazard, exposure and vulnerability; United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, Sendai Framework Terminology on Disaster Risk Reduction, 2017, entries Hazard, Disaster, Disaster Risk, Exposure, Vulnerability and Capacity, consulted 2 November 2026; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, chapter 3, Our Changing Earth, printed pp. 12–14.]

title: Understanding Hazards, Disasters and the Components of Disaster Risk

body:
Capacity is the ability to manage risk

Communities are not merely passive recipients of disasters. They possess resources, institutions, knowledge and relationships that can prevent losses or make adverse conditions easier to manage.

Capacity includes trained personnel, functioning hospitals, communication networks, public shelters, local knowledge, community organisations and financial resources. Coping capacity refers more specifically to the ability to manage adverse conditions using available skills and resources.

A village may have a flood-prone location but also possess an effective warning arrangement, accessible shelters and volunteers who assist people with limited mobility. These capacities can reduce the consequences of flooding.

Resilience: maintaining and restoring essential functions

Resilience is the ability of a system, community or society exposed to hazards to resist, absorb, respond to and recover from their effects in a timely and effective manner.

Resilience includes both the ability to withstand disruption and the ability to restore essential functions afterwards. A community with alternative drinking-water arrangements, strong social cooperation and an effective recovery plan may regain normal services sooner than an equally exposed community without these arrangements.

Capacity and resilience are related but distinct. Capacity refers to available strengths and resources. Resilience describes how effectively a community or system withstands, adapts to and recovers from disturbance. Strong capacity can improve resilience, but the 2 terms are not interchangeable.

Why disaster risk changes over time

Risk is not permanent. Construction in a floodplain may increase exposure. Deteriorating buildings may increase vulnerability. Public awareness, improved drainage, safer land use and better evacuation arrangements may reduce risk. Climate-related changes can also alter the frequency or intensity of some hazards.

Consequently, disaster-risk reduction must be integrated into ordinary development decisions. A project that creates new buildings or roads without considering local hazards can unintentionally create new disaster risk.

Intensive and extensive disaster risk

Disaster risk can be classified according to the typical severity and frequency of hazardous events. This distinction concerns the pattern of risk, not merely the geographical area involved.

FeatureIntensive disaster riskExtensive disaster risk
Typical severityHighRelatively low
Typical frequencyMedium to lowHigh
Typical exampleSevere earthquake causing widespread destructionRepeated local flooding affecting homes and livelihoods
Important featurePotentially catastrophic losses in a major eventAccumulating losses from recurring events

Intensive risk is associated with high-severity disasters, such as a major earthquake affecting a vulnerable city. Extensive risk is associated with more frequent, generally lower-severity events, such as repeated local floods or small landslides.

Extensive events should not be dismissed as unimportant. Repeated repairs, interruptions to work, damaged crops and lost household income can produce substantial cumulative hardship. Similarly, an intensive disaster may cause consequences far beyond the location where the original hazard occurred.

Cascading effects: one disruption causes another

A cascading effect occurs when the consequences of an initial hazardous event trigger further disruptions. These secondary effects can increase losses even where the original physical hazard has already ended.

Consider an earthquake that damages electricity infrastructure. Power interruptions may stop water pumps. Water shortages can then affect households and health facilities. If roads and communications are also damaged, restoring these services becomes more difficult.

The Gujarat earthquake of 26 January 2001 illustrates why infrastructure connections matter: damage was reported to electricity, water and communication systems as well as buildings.

Cascading consequences are not inevitable. Backup power, alternative water supplies, protected communication systems and coordinated repair work can prevent or reduce secondary disruptions. This shows how capacity and resilience operate in practice.

Residual risk remains after precautions

Residual risk is the risk that remains even after effective risk-reduction measures have been implemented. Improved drainage does not guarantee that every possible flood can be prevented. A strengthened building may still face an unusually severe hazard.

Because residual risk cannot always be eliminated, communities still need warning systems, preparedness, emergency assistance and recovery arrangements.

Prelims focus

  • Capacity includes resources, knowledge, institutions and social cooperation.
  • Resilience includes the ability to resist, absorb, respond to and recover from disruption.
  • Intensive risk: high severity, generally medium-to-low frequency.
  • Extensive risk: relatively low severity, high frequency.
  • Cascading effects: an initial disruption produces additional disruptions.
  • Trap: Extensive risk does not mean a single event must affect a larger area than an intensive disaster.

[Sources: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, Sendai Framework Terminology on Disaster Risk Reduction, 2017, entries Capacity, Resilience, Intensive Disaster Risk, Extensive Disaster Risk, Hazard and Residual Risk, consulted 2 November 2026; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, chapter 3, Our Changing Earth, printed p. 14, Gujarat earthquake case study; Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, section 2, definition of resilience.]

title: Capacity, Resilience, Intensive and Extensive Risk, and Cascading Effects

body:
Disaster management begins before the event

Disaster management is not limited to rescue operations after an earthquake or flood. It is a continuous process of planning, coordinating and implementing measures that reduce risk, prepare people for emergencies, respond to actual events and support recovery.

The actions taken before a disaster are often grouped as prevention, mitigation and preparedness. Although these activities may occur together, they answer different questions.

Prevention, mitigation and preparedness

TermMain purposeExample
PreventionAvoid creating or experiencing a particular disaster riskProhibiting settlement in an identified high-risk area
MitigationReduce the harmful consequences of a hazardImproving drainage or strengthening vulnerable buildings
PreparednessDevelop readiness to act effectively when danger threatensPlanning evacuation routes, conducting drills and maintaining emergency supplies

Prevention aims to avoid harm

Prevention consists of activities and measures intended to avoid existing or new disaster risks. For example, keeping new residential development away from an extremely hazardous location can prevent that particular exposure from arising.

Prevention does not imply that every natural hazard can be stopped. Earthquakes cannot generally be prevented. However, particular risks arising from unsafe siting or avoidable exposure may be prevented.

Mitigation aims to lessen harm

Mitigation reduces the expected severity or consequences of a hazard that may still occur. Keeping stormwater drains clear can reduce local flooding. Protecting vulnerable buildings and following suitable construction standards can reduce likely damage from hazardous events.

Mitigation is especially important where complete avoidance is impossible. In disaster management, mitigation means reducing disaster impacts. In climate-change policy, the same word usually refers to reducing greenhouse-gas emissions. The meaning depends on the context.

Preparedness creates readiness

Preparedness develops the knowledge, skills, arrangements and resources needed to anticipate, respond to and recover from disasters. It includes identifying safe shelters, arranging transport for people who need assistance, maintaining communication channels, storing essential supplies and conducting mock drills.

Preparing an evacuation plan does not remove a cyclone hazard. It enables people to act before the hazard reaches them. Thus, an evacuation drill is primarily a preparedness measure, while measures that reduce the likely damage to a building are primarily mitigation measures.

Early warning connects information with action

An early warning system provides information about an approaching or developing hazard so that people and authorities can act in time. An effective system needs more than an accurate forecast: the warning must reach the affected people, be understood and lead to suitable action.

Effective multi-hazard early warning systems are built around 4 connected elements:

  1. Disaster-risk knowledge: understanding which hazards threaten particular people and places.
  2. Monitoring, analysis and forecasting: detecting hazards and assessing their likely development.
  3. Warning dissemination and communication: delivering timely, understandable information to those at risk.
  4. Preparedness and response capability: ensuring people and institutions can act on the warning.

A warning that never reaches a remote village may provide little protection. Likewise, a warning received without a known shelter or evacuation arrangement may not lead to effective action. Communication must therefore account for language, accessibility, local conditions and available means of transport.

In India, the National Disaster Management Authority's SACHET system supports the dissemination of geographically relevant disaster alerts through multiple communication channels. Hazard information may originate from specialised agencies, including the India Meteorological Department for weather-related hazards, the Central Water Commission for river-flood information and the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services for relevant ocean-related warnings.

Basic precautions for the public

Precautions vary according to the hazard. The following examples concern ordinary public safety rather than specialist emergency-response procedures.

  • Earthquake: If indoors, drop down, take cover under sturdy furniture where possible and hold on. Stay away from glass and heavy objects. Avoid lifts during evacuation.
  • Flood: Follow official warnings and move to a safer location when advised. Do not walk or drive through floodwater or approach damaged electrical installations.
  • Cyclone: Secure loose items when conditions are safe, monitor authoritative warnings and evacuate promptly if instructed.
  • Heatwave: Maintain hydration, limit unnecessary exposure to extreme heat and give particular attention to people who may need assistance.
  • Industrial accident: Avoid approaching the affected area and follow instructions from the responsible public authorities.

Prevention avoids a risk; mitigation reduces its impact; preparedness improves the ability to act. All 3 are needed because not every hazard can be eliminated.

Prelims focus

  • Restricting settlement in a dangerous location is an example of prevention.
  • Reducing likely damage through protective measures is mitigation.
  • Mock drills, emergency supplies and evacuation plans are preparedness.
  • Effective early warning requires risk knowledge, forecasting, communication and response capability.
  • Trap: Issuing a forecast alone does not complete an effective warning-and-response process.

[Sources: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, Sendai Framework Terminology on Disaster Risk Reduction, 2017, entries Prevention, Mitigation and Preparedness, consulted 2 November 2026; World Meteorological Organization, Early Warnings for All, Four Essential Pillars of Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems, consulted 2 November 2026; National Disaster Management Authority, SACHET National Disaster Alert Portal, About and Dos and Don'ts, portal updated 15 October 2026, consulted 2 November 2026; National Institute of Disaster Management, National Disaster Risk Reduction Communication Toolkit, Earthquake Health poster; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, chapter 3, Our Changing Earth, printed p. 14.]
